name: Furosemide
summary: A high-ceiling loop diuretic that blocks sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb; first-line for acute pulmonary edema and symptomatic congestion in heart failure.
mechanism: Inhibits the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, producing potent natriuresis and diuresis.

pharmacokinetics.halfLife: ~1.5–2 h (healthy); prolonged in renal impairment and heart failure

dosing.adult: Edema/heart failure: 20–40 mg once daily oral or IV, titrated to effect; acute pulmonary edema: 40 mg IV (repeat as needed)

safety.pregnancy: Category C; used when benefit outweighs risk
safety.lactation: Small amounts in milk; may suppress lactation
warnings: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and hypovolemia — the classic triad of loop-diuretic excess
Ototoxicity with rapid IV push or with aminoglycosides
Sulfonamide cross-reactivity — caution in sulfa allergy
safety.overdose: Dehydration, electrolyte depletion, and hypotension; replace volume and electrolytes.

indications: Edema of hepatic or renal origin
clinicalPearls: Loop diuretics have a threshold effect — the dose must exceed the diuretic threshold to work, so escalation is stepwise.
Oral bioavailability is ~50%, so IV dose is roughly half the oral dose for equivalent effect.
good: Acute congestion and diuresis in renal-impaired patients who do not respond to thiazides.
bad: Anuria, significant electrolyte depletion, or concurrent aminoglycosides (ototoxicity).

provenance.notes: Curated from standard pharmacology references (Goodman & Gilman, Katzung, Lexicomp-level standard facts). Values omitted where not confidently known — nothing invented.
